source: Hambrick, Macnamara & Oswald (2020) Is the deliberate practice view defensible? (full text via PMC)
finding: Reliability-corrected reanalysis of Hambrick 2014: DP explains 34% of reliable variance in chess and 29.9% in music. The text says this is not enough to support the claim that DP largely accounts for expertise differences.
numbers: chess 34%, music 29.9% of reliable variance. Text confirms Macnamara 2014 has a 2018 corrigendum (Psychol Sci 29:1202-1204) and Burgoyne 2016 has a 2018 corrigendum (Intelligence 71:92-96).
limits: Secondary reading of Hambrick 2014. The corrigenda themselves (what changed in Games k, N) were not retrievable, so Gap 3 Games k/N stays open.
agent_relevance: Use 34% as the prior: practice amount explains about a third of reliable variance.

source: Hambrick et al. (2020), re-analysis of Ericsson & Harwell (2019) correlations
finding: Ericsson and Harwell's own meta-analytic numbers show coach-guided deliberate practice is not a significantly stronger predictor than self-directed purposeful practice (goal plus feedback).
numbers: r deliberate = .56 (k=8), r purposeful = .51 (k=6), r combined = .54 (k=14); difference n.s., p=.64. Corrected rc with reliability .80-.90 gave about .62-.76 (38.7%-58.1% variance) in their Table 3.
limits: Correlational, self-report practice; k small. Direction favours DP but not reliably.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the teacher component adds little beyond goal plus feedback. For an agent, specific goal plus feedback is the working definition; a coach layer is not shown to matter.

source: Hambrick et al. (2020) on Burgoyne et al. (2016) chess meta-analysis, skill-band moderator
finding: Fluid intelligence correlated more strongly with chess rating in lower-skill players than in higher-skill players, but skill level was confounded with age (lower-skill samples were youth).
numbers: avg r = .32 (lower skill) vs .14 (higher skill). Age confound stated by the authors.
limits: Seen via Hambrick 2020 text, not the Burgoyne primary (paywalled). Gap 3 chess-only effect by band: only this partial answer.
agent_relevance: Ceiling hint (Gap 8): ability matters less at high skill, but the evidence is confounded.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: A prompt-only agent with a memory of its own written reflections improved over repeated trials on ALFWorld without weight updates. The ReAct-only baseline stopped improving between trials 6 and 7.
numbers: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 ALFWorld tasks within 12 consecutive trials; paper reports +22% absolute on ALFWorld, +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval over strong baselines.
limits: Uses a binary success signal from the environment (oracle-like evaluator). The text shows the no-reflection baseline plateauing; a saturation point for Reflexion itself is not stated.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: yes, a practice-like gain across episodes exists with note memory only, but it depends on a reliable external success signal.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Self-correction improves only when an oracle label says the answer is wrong. Without it, extra rounds make accuracy fall or stay flat.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 base, 75.1 / 74.7 after rounds 1 / 2; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 / 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 / 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 79.5 / 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 / 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 / 90.0. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5 / 36.5. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
limits: Table row alignment partly garbled by text extraction; 2023-era models; prompts taken from prior papers.
agent_relevance: Gap 2/6: Reflexion-type gains are largely a feedback-quality effect. A scaffold needs an external check, not self-judgment, or it can lose accuracy.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez & Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs really improve by self-critiquing their own plans?
finding: On Blocksworld, GPT-4 critiquing GPT-4 plans is worse than critiquing with a sound external verifier because the LLM verifier gives many false positives. Binary vs detailed feedback made no big difference.
numbers: 100 instances: generator only 40/100; LLM+LLM with backprompting 55/100 (3.48 iterations avg); LLM+VAL sound verifier 88/100 (4.18 iterations).
limits: One domain, GPT-4 only, n=100. Self-critique still beat no backprompting here (55 vs 40).
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the external sound verifier gave most of the gain; the LLM verifier about a third. Verifier quality is the lever.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning in LLM-Modulo frameworks
finding: With an external verifier backprompting (reported from Valmeekam 2023c), Blocks World reaches 82% within 15 rounds and Logistics 70%. On obfuscated Mystery Blocks World it stays near 10%, since the LLM cannot propose plausible candidates.
numbers: Blocks World 82% (15 rounds), Logistics 70%, Mystery BW about 10%.
limits: Position paper; figures are reported from other studies, not re-run. Gains need a sound verifier and a generator with non-trivial base rate.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: verifiers help where candidates are already plausible. Where the generator is near zero, verification cannot rescue it.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with LLMs
finding: Ablations of a prompt-only lifelong agent (no weight updates): a random curriculum cuts discovered items by 93%; removing self-verification cuts them by 73%; removing the skill library makes progress plateau late.
numbers: Discovered items: random curriculum -93%; no self-verification -73%; no skill library: late plateau (no number in text). A manual curriculum was worse than the automatic one.
limits: Minecraft only. The curriculum is chosen by GPT-4 from agent state, so it is adaptive, not merely ordered; the ablation confounds ordering with adaptivity.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: best inference-only evidence that state-based task choice matters a lot, but not a clean weakness-targeting vs random test at equal budget.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Self-Evolving Curriculum for LLM reasoning (SEC)
finding: RL fine-tuning where a bandit picks the difficulty category with the highest learning gain beats random sampling and easy-to-hard ordering at the same training budget, mostly on out-of-distribution sets for the small model.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B OOD: Countdown 0.48 random vs 0.54 SEC (ordered 0.32); Zebra 0.29 to 0.35; AIME24 0.075 to 0.10. Ordered curriculum was often worse than random (Countdown ID 0.551 vs 0.859).
limits: Trains weights (GRPO); not inference-only. Single runs in the table text.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/7: closest model analogue of targeted vs unguided practice at equal steps: gain is real but modest, and easy-first ordering can hurt. A prompt-only version is untested.

source: Chen et al. (2025) SEC, 7B vs 3B comparison
finding: The curriculum gain shrinks with the stronger base model. The authors say a stronger model already handles a broad range of problems, so explicit curriculum matters less.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B: Countdown OOD random 0.512 vs SEC 0.514; Zebra OOD 0.32 to 0.36 (+11%); AIME 0.14 to 0.18 (+27% relative). 3B: Countdown +13%, AIME +33% relative.
limits: Relative gains on small absolute numbers; two sizes of one family only.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a ceiling effect shows in models too. Expect scaffold benefit to shrink on tasks the base model already solves; hard tasks still gain.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: Self-feedback gains are large on style and preference tasks and near zero where the first output is already strong or the model cannot tell it is wrong. Returns diminish across iterations.
numbers: Sentiment reversal GPT-4 3.8 to 36.2; code optimisation GPT-4 92.9 to 93.1 (+0.2), ChatGPT 74.8 to 75.0; math GPT-3.5 64.1 to 64.1 (0). Constrained generation 29.0 to 49.7 after 3 iterations, with falling marginal gain. ChatGPT feedback said 'everything looks good' for 94% of instances; an external signal flagging wrong math answers gave 5%+.
limits: Metrics differ per task; 2023 models; low bases (3.8) make part of the gain a floor effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: ceiling visible (+0.2 at base 93). Gap 2: iteration gains saturate within about 3 rounds.

source: Song et al. (2025) Mind the gap: examining the self-improvement capabilities of LLMs
finding: Self-improvement is governed by the generation-verification gap. The gap grows with pretraining FLOPs for good verifiers, but iterating shrinks it to zero in a handful of rounds, independent of model size, and diversity falls.
numbers: Relative GV-gap rises monotonically with log pretraining FLOPs; iterative gap saturates to 0 in a few rounds; most models show no self-improvement on tasks beyond their own reasoning or planning ability.
limits: Numbers are in figures, not text. Framework is verify-filter-distil (weights), but the verifier finding applies to prompt-only loops.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 (saturation quickly) and Gap 8 (stronger models self-improve more via better verification, only on tasks within reach).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: A prompt-only agent that collects its own trials, extracts insights, and retrieves similar past successes improves with the number of experiences. Random retrieval of past trajectories is clearly worse than task-similar retrieval.
numbers: ExpeL final: HotpotQA 39.0%, ALFWorld 59.0%; insights-only vs retrieval-only 36%/31% HotpotQA and 50%/55% ALFWorld; WebShop 37%/38%. Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER: ReAct 58, ExpeL transfer 65-70. Insights extracted only from the few-shot examples gave no advantage over ReAct.
limits: Ablation table columns partly garbled in extraction. GPT-4 used for insight extraction; hand-crafted insights were worse than LLM ones.
agent_relevance: Gap 2/5/9: experience and abstraction both matter, and practice must produce new feedback; re-reading given examples does nothing. A random-example control (Gap 5) exists here and loses.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Inducing reusable workflows from past successful runs (offline or online, no weight updates) raises success and cuts steps. The gain grows as train-test distance grows.
numbers: Relative success +24.6% (Mind2Web) and +51.1% (WebArena); online AWM beats baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as train-test gaps widen.
limits: Web benchmarks only; online mode relies on the agent's own success judgment, so errors can be stored.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a note memory of what worked gives sizeable gains on a shifted distribution. Gap 1: no weakness-targeted arm.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus 20 datasets x 14 models: CoT helps mostly on math and logic tasks; on MMLU the benefit is almost all on questions containing an equals sign.
numbers: Up to 95% of the CoT gain on MMLU is attributed to questions with symbolic content; a symbolic solver beat CoT on those.
limits: CoT only; not a practice study. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 8/9: scaffold benefit is task-conditional. Expect near-zero gain from extra thinking on recall items and large gain only where a procedure exists.

source: Southwick, Harwell, Wright, Olsen et al. (2026) Not all practice is created equal: longitudinal evidence from over 40,000 chess players (Psychological Science), Europe PMC record
finding: Only the bibliographic record was reached; no full text or supplement. Whether the 3.61x learning-efficiency result survives controls for motivation or prior rating (Gap 4) could not be checked.
numbers: Record only: title, authors, 2026. No new numbers. (Earlier critique: N=44,213, over 90% of time on games, 3.61x efficiency, from the abstract.)
limits: No full text found. Web search budget was exhausted, so the paper or any preprint could not be located.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. Treat 3.61x as observational and unadjusted until the supplement is read.
